Performance only: a tone is a reading, not evidence of how anyone spoke (L-jaunt-voices-3578). Keyed <part>:<id>.

scripts.opening:opening:
[measured] Fort Dearborn, Building by Building.

[short pause] It is Friday, 14 August 1812. This is the last full day of the first Fort Dearborn. The United States built this fort in 1803. Captain John Whistler and his soldiers marched here from Detroit. [short pause] They built it out of logs on the south bank of the Chicago River. In 1808 Whistler drew a picture of every building. Since 1810 the fort's leader has been Captain Nathan Heald. [short pause] He has more than sixty soldiers.

[short pause] In June the United States went to war with Britain. Five days ago, a general sent an order: leave the fort. Tomorrow morning the soldiers will march out of the gate. [short pause] Today everyone is packing up.

[short pause] There are twelve stops, from sunrise to sunset. By tomorrow night, all but one of these buildings will be burned. [short pause] Watch for the one that lasts.
scripts.stop:the-fort: [measured] It is 14 August 1812, at sunrise. [short pause] This is the first Fort Dearborn, seen from outside. Captain Whistler's soldiers came to this bend in the river in 1803. They built the whole fort out of logs with their own hands. [short pause] A visitor in 1809 called it the neatest and best wooden fort in the country. There are soldiers' houses around a square. There are two tall gun towers at opposite corners. Two rows of log walls go all the way around. [short pause] Now the order has come to leave. Tomorrow everyone inside will go. [short pause] Today is their last full day here.
scripts.stop:the-gate: [measured] It is six in the morning, at the main gate on the south side. [short pause] A girl who lived here remembered that the gates shut at sunset. Look at the two rows of log walls. If an enemy climbed over the first wall, he would be stuck in a narrow space. [short pause] Soldiers in the towers could fire at him there. Whistler built this fort to hold off an attack. But nobody plans to stay and fight now. The order is to march out, and this is the gate they will use. [short pause] Walk through the gate and step inside to where the soldiers live.
scripts.stop:soldiers: [measured] It is seven in the morning, just inside the gate. [short pause] The soldiers' houses stand on both sides. They are two stories tall, with porches facing the open square. The first soldiers here built the fort themselves. When their time in the army ended, they all signed up again. [short pause] This fort was very far from anywhere. Whistler wrote that he had sixty-six men but not enough clothes for all of them. He even said the only flute for the band had been lost. [short pause] This morning the soldiers are packing for the long march to Fort Wayne.
scripts.stop:commandant: [measured] It is half past eight, on the open square. [short pause] In the middle stands a tall flagpole. On the east side is the house of the fort's leader, Captain Nathan Heald. In 1811 he brought his new wife, Rebekah, to live here. [short pause] A book says she and Mrs. Helm played a game like badminton here last spring. In May, the Healds' baby boy was born but did not live. The order to leave came on 9 August. [short pause] It was read out loud the next morning, right here. The officers asked Heald to stay and make the fort stronger. [short pause] But Heald chose to obey the order.
scripts.stop:officers: [measured] It is ten o'clock, at the officers' house, across from the leader's house. [short pause] Three men live here. Lieutenant Linai Helm is second in charge. His wife, Margaret, is the stepdaughter of John Kinzie, the trader across the river. Ensign George Ronan is the youngest officer. He came straight from army school. [short pause] Dr. Isaac Van Voorhis is the fort's young doctor, only twenty-two. Last fall he wrote that one day millions of people would live here. He was right. [short pause] Sadly, Ronan and the doctor will not live through tomorrow, and Helm will be taken prisoner.
scripts.stop:magazine: [measured] It is eleven o'clock, on the north side. [short pause] Ahead is the magazine, where the gunpowder is kept. It is a small building made of brick, in a fort made of logs. Next to it is a gun tower and a small side gate. [short pause] When the fort burns, this little brick building will be the only one left standing. But the fort's extra gunpowder is not here anymore. Last night it was carried out in secret to the north-east corner. [short pause] Then it was dropped down a well.
scripts.stop:covered-way: [measured] It is noon, at the north-east corner. [short pause] From here a covered path once ran down to the river. It let soldiers get water safely during an attack. A well was dug inside it. Last night the soldiers threw the extra gunpowder and broken guns down the well. [short pause] They poured the whiskey into the river. Captain Heald did not want anyone to use those things against them. It was no secret. By morning, people said, the river water tasted like whiskey. [short pause] Now everyone outside the fort knows the extra guns are gone.
scripts.stop:merchants: [measured] It is half past one, outside the log walls on the south-east side. [short pause] Here stood a store, a garden, and a shop where the soldiers' guns were fixed. One trader was allowed to sell things to the soldiers. Since January, that was John Kinzie and his partner. Behind you rises the south-east gun tower. [short pause] Whistler's drawing put the towers on two opposite corners. A book written forty years later remembered them both on the south side. People do not always remember things the same way. [short pause] South of here, the gardens are full of food nobody will stay to eat.
scripts.stop:gardens: [measured] It is three in the afternoon, in the leader's gardens, south of the fort. [short pause] In the early years, people grew melons, fruit and vegetables here. Whistler had all the bushes cleared for a long way around the fort, so nobody could sneak up. [short pause] Past the gardens is a big open field of grass and a line of trees by the river. Tomorrow the soldiers and families will go the other way. [short pause] They will walk east to the lake, then south along the beach.
scripts.stop:agency: [measured] It is half past four, west of the fort, among the government buildings. [short pause] There is a trading house, a few homes, a bakery and the stables. The trading house is the government's own store. Today Captain Heald gave away all the goods in the store. [short pause] His report says he "delivered the Indians all the goods in the factory store". He also gave away food the soldiers could not carry. Blankets, cloth and paints went out the door. In April, the townspeople made one log house stronger. [short pause] They boarded up its porches and cut holes to look out, and guards watched at night. [short pause] Now the store shelves are empty.
scripts.stop:wharf: [measured] It is six in the evening, at the dock below the river bank. [short pause] Here boats tied up and the fort's supplies were unloaded. In 1808 Whistler said the fort was safe from a surprise attack. He said only one thing was in the way: the houses across the river. [short pause] The biggest of those houses belongs to John Kinzie. His family will not march with the soldiers tomorrow. They will leave by boat. [short pause] Walk along the bank and look at the house as the sun goes down on the fort's last night.
scripts.stop:across-the-river: [measured] It is sunset. [short pause] Across the river is John Kinzie's house, with three more houses to the west. Kinzie sells to the soldiers and lives close enough to shout to the gate. Behind you, the gates are shutting at sunset, for the last time. [short pause] Tomorrow at nine in the morning they will open. The band will play slow, sad music, and the soldiers will walk out. The next day the fort will be set on fire. Only the brick magazine will last. [short pause] The army will come back in 1816 and build a new fort here.
scripts.ending:burned: [solemnly] On 15 August 1812 the soldiers and families marched out of the gate. Captain Heald wrote later that the warriors set fire to the fort and left, taking prisoners with them. Seven months later, a visitor found the brick magazine still standing. [short pause] Everything else Whistler built had burned down. For four years the place was quiet and empty. Then the army came back in 1816 and built a new fort on the same ground. [short pause] To follow the soldiers out of the gate on the morning of the 15th, take the jaunt The Battle of Fort Dearborn.
